question: Can a federated ridge regression, which aggregates exact sufficient statistics and exposes readable coefficients, match or beat a FedAvg-trained MLP for next-hour household load forecasting?
method: Hourly mean Global_active_power with lag and calendar features; chronological 80/20 split; training part divided into contiguous time-block clients; both models trained federatedly and evaluated on the same held-out test period.

dataset.name: UCI Individual Household Electric Power Consumption (resampled to hourly)

baseline: FedAvg-trained scikit-learn MLPRegressor (64-32 ReLU, Adam, local partial_fit, 20 rounds of 1 local epoch, sample-weighted averaging of weights across 5 clients), on the original lag and calendar features.
improved: Federated ridge regression on extended features (original lags and calendar, rolling 24h/168h means, 24h std, weekly same-hour mean, hour-of-day and day-of-week indicators, and hour x lag_1 / hour x lag_24 interactions). Each client sends only X'X and X'y once; the server sums them and solves; lambda chosen by leave-one-block-out CV on the training blocks.
notes: Single chronological split of one household series; the clients are time blocks, so they are non-IID by construction. Both models use the same rows and the same test period; the baseline inputs are unchanged. The improvement comes only from the richer linear feature map for ridge, with lambda chosen by leave-one-block-out CV on training data. Only the MLP is randomized; ridge is deterministic, so its seed spread is zero. The MLP is untuned, so the comparison is not a fully tuned benchmark. The motivating paper's model and results were not available, so no paper numbers are reproduced.
